newsitem.title: UK: British soldier hurt by suspected IRA bomb.
newsitem.headline: British soldier hurt by suspected IRA bomb.

text.p: An off-duty British soldier was wounded in a suspected IRA booby-trap bomb attack in the country town of Ballynahinch in Northern Ireland early on Sunday.
Security sources said he was slightly injured when his parked car exploded as he and two colleagues were close to it. "As he walked forward to check it, it exploded," a police spokesman said.
The explosion appeared to be the latest in a string of attacks on soldiers and police mounted by the banned Irish Republican Army, British security sources said.
The off-duty soldiers, believed to be from a nearby army base at Ballykinlar in County Down, had left the vehicle in a car park late on Saturday night.
"It was really only by vigilance that lives were saved," a police source told Reuters.
Ballynahinch is some 20 miles (30 kms) south of Belfast and and a short distance from Downpatrick where mortars were fired at security force patrol last week.
In the north-western town of Dungiven, security forces seized a home-made projectile and rifle and arrested five men.
A police spokesman said that arrested followed "suspicious activity" at Main Street, where the town's fortified police station is located, but he did not give any details.
The missile was a "PRIG", a propelled recoiless improvised grenade, a common IRA weapon used to attack bases and patrolling security vehicles.
Soldiers and police have been on full alert in recent weeks after a sudden surge in IRA hostilities and revenge attacks by pro-British Loyalist extremists.
Britain says that the IRA, which abandoned a 17 month truce in February 1996, is intensifying its campaign to goad its Loyalist foess into abandoning a 27 month ceasefire.
The IRA is fighting to end British rule and achieve an all- Ireland state. Loyalists killed minority Catholic nationalists in a campaign to safeguard rule from London.

Police have said three recent attacks on Catholics were carried out by Protestant extremists loyal to Britain but have not said if actions were sanctioned by the groups that called the Loyalist ceasefire.

Britain says the IRA must call a ceasefire to get its Sinn Fein a seat in current multi-party peace talks. It condemns the Protestant attacks but says it does not believe the Loyalist guerrilla forces have abandoned their truce.

Former U.S. senator George Mitchell is due to re-open round table talks between most of the province's bitterly divided parties in Belfast on Monday in a bid to breathe life into a battered three-year peace process.
The security and political climate has worsened considerably since the talks, which are sponsored by Britain and Ireland, went into recess in the runup to Christmas.
Political parties show no sign of ending a deadlock that has stalled progress in the Mitchell talks since their launch last June.

Protestant mainstream parties say they will challenged British Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Patrick Mayhew to state whether politicians linked to Loyalist guerrillas should be expelled from the talks in retaliation for Loyalist violence.
No-one has been killed in IRA attacks since October when the guerrillas struck with two car bombs killing one soldier inside Britain's chief military garrison at Lisburn, south of Belfast.
But the quickening pace of IRA attacks and mounting strains on the Loyalist ceasefire have fuelled fears that the province could slide back into a cycle of deadly "blow for blow" violence.
